preamble: * Clues so marked refer to a familiar poem

clue.text: Scots have, taking in variety of ebb and flaw, their own farthing?

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one word goes into the middle of the other

parts.note: the Scots form of the verb have

indicators.note: a variety of something is a different version of it, so these letters come out in another order

parts.note: the letters of the two words, without the 'and'

explanation.surface: A Scotsman, weathering ebbing tides and squalls, hangs on to every last farthing of his own.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled letters go inside HAE between the A and the E. A bawbee was an old Scottish halfpenny, so half of one is a farthing, the quarter-penny coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A half bawbee was a Scottish coin worth a quarter of a penny, the Scots counterpart of the English farthing.

clue.text: Artificial pitch makes the flower of Cornwall fight

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Fal runs through Cornwall
a set-to is a fight or scrap

explanation.surface: Someone claims the finest bloom of Cornwall stirs up a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; read it as flow-er, something that flows, and it is a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Falsetto is the unnaturally high singing voice a man produces above his normal range, an artificial register.

clue.text: The sea's near and I'm off

definitions.note: a possessive standing for an adjective: belonging to the sea

indicators.note: something gone off has gone bad or wrong, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone at the coast announces that the water is close by and they are setting off.
explanation.definitionFit: Marine means relating to or found in the sea, so a marine creature is one of the ocean's own.

clue.text: Beast leading nation to zero growth

definitions.note: a cryptic description: put in front of the word nation, it makes a term for zero growth
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the word that, leading the word nation, makes stagnation, an economy with no growth

explanation.surface: An animal heads a country into economic standstill.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a politician driving the country to recession; the second half really describes a word that turns 'nation' into stagnation.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag is an adult male deer, a familiar wild animal of British forests and parks.

clue.text: 4 may perform what are played there?

definitions.text: 4 may perform what are played there?

parts.note: surface reading: the deer of 4 down putting on some act
setter's reading: 4 down may form a gathering (a stag do), and this is what gets played at such a gathering

explanation.walkthrough: 4 down is STAG; before 'party' it makes a stag party, the British pre-wedding night out, and the answer is the games played at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Party games such as charades or musical chairs are the amusements played at a social gathering.

clue.text: Surgeon upset by a new boss

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hospital surgeon is put out by the arrival of a new head of department.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones is old slang for a doctor, especially a surgeon, from the days when amputation was common work.

clue.text: Jungle dweller gives Dr Grace a pound

parts.note: MO, medical officer, a doctor
W G Grace, the famous Victorian cricketer, known by his initials
L is the abbreviation for pound, with I as one, 'a'

explanation.surface: A jungle inhabitant hands the cricketing doctor W G Grace a pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: W G Grace was himself a doctor, which makes the surface 'Dr Grace' fit; here Dr and Grace are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Mowgli is the boy raised by wolves who lives in the forest in Kipling's The Jungle Book.

clue.text: * Low pole, none at town tonight …

definitions.note: the thing of which there is none: the poem's town has a moonless night

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
N, the north pole

explanation.surface: Cattle lowing, a pole, and a town with nothing happening tonight.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem is Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood, which opens on a 'moonless night in the small town'. The dots run on into 14 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's night is moonless, so this heavenly body is the one thing absent over the town tonight.

clue.text: Celebration in the first act, a problem not experienced by Miss 20

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: the first act of a play is Act I
a gala is a festive celebration
taken as written

explanation.surface: A party staged during the opening act, and some trouble that a certain young lady avoids.
explanation.walkthrough: GALA goes inside ACT I, just after its A. Miss 20 is Polly Garter of Under Milk Wood, forever nursing babies.
explanation.definitionFit: Agalactia is the failure of a mother to produce milk, never a trouble for the poem's constantly nursing Polly Garter.

clue.text: Offensive Australian on the left-hand page from the start

parts.note: an offensive Australian slang word for an Aboriginal person
VO is verso, the left-hand page of a book

explanation.surface: A rude Australian appears on the left page of a book, right from the beginning.
explanation.definitionFit: Ab ovo is Latin for 'from the egg', meaning from the very beginning of a story or process.

clue.text: * The sea takes a smack at Hope and Crosby

definitions.note: not a synonym: the poem's epithet for the sea

parts.note: a smack is a small sailing vessel that works the sea for a catch
Bob Hope, the comedian
Bing Crosby, the singer, Hope's partner in the Road films

explanation.surface: The sea lashes out at the comedy double act of Bob Hope and Bing Crosby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a blow; it is the boat. Under Milk Wood describes the 'sloeblack, slow, black, crowblack, fishingboat-bobbing sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas's compound epithet pictures the sea at Llareggub dotted with small vessels rising and falling on the waves.

clue.text: * Opening time gong: spirit tips off Matthew to ask at pub for a mixed one

indicators.note: something mixed has been stirred up, so its letters come in a new order
with the tips taken off, a word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
gong is slang for a medal or honour, such as the OBE
gin is a spirit
taken as written, before trimming
to beg is to ask
an inn is a pub
one more of the spirit already named

explanation.surface: The bell rings at opening time and a drinker, taking the hint, goes to the bar to order a mixed gin.
explanation.walkthrough: These are the opening words of Under Milk Wood. 'Opening time gong' looks like one picture, but 'Opening' alone is the definition; an OBE is a British honour, nicknamed a gong.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the famous first line of Dylan Thomas's play for voices, its opening words.

clue.text: See 12
See 12
* … which is returning about the first and second bell, possibly

parts.note: continuing from 8 down: the moonless night in the town, which the poem says is this colour

parts.words: returning about the first and second bell, possibly
parts.note: setter's reading: a book that goes back over the first and second (the Old and New Testaments), and the colour of a church bell, perhaps

explanation.surface: Continuing 8 down: a bell rung first and second, then rung again.
explanation.walkthrough: Under Milk Wood's night is 'starless and bible-black'. The wordplay is allusive; the Bible covers the first and second Testaments, and a bell may be black.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas coined the compound for the deep darkness of the night, as black as the binding of a Bible.

clue.text: Long girdle going round 16?

indicators.note: letters going round are spun about and come to rest in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lengthy belt wraps around the film star of 16.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the definition works by example: the 16 across star is one kind of golden girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A blonde bombshell is a dazzling fair-haired beauty, which is exactly what a golden girl suggests.

clue.text: A cut from Hobbema's work accepted by Joan or Jean Harlow

indicators.note: what is accepted by someone is taken in, so it sits inside

parts.note: Joan Blondell, the Hollywood actress

indicators.note: worked letters have been reworked into a different shape
what is cut from something is removed from it

parts.note: taken as written; one A is then removed

explanation.surface: A detail from a Hobbema painting is admired by one Hollywood actress or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is the letter cut, not an article; Hobbema was a Dutch landscape painter, so 'work' poses as his painting when it is the anagram signal. Joan Blondell and Jean Harlow were both 1930s Hollywood stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Harlow, the platinum-haired 1930s film star, was the original screen example of a dazzling sexy fair-haired woman.

clue.text: * I have two wives and fear keeping one in the place

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it within, so the other pieces sit inside

parts.note: dread is fear
a, one
ib., short for ibidem, Latin for in the same place

explanation.surface: A bigamist admits his fear of keeping one of his wives in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken in character: Dai Bread, the baker of Under Milk Wood, has two wives, Mrs Dai Bread One and Mrs Dai Bread Two.
explanation.definitionFit: Dai Bread is the poem's baker, famous for living with two wives at once, so the line is his self-description.

clue.text: Hungry for Le Mesurier's part that's not to be shortened

indicators.note: only a part of the name is wanted, so letters at both ends are dropped
a shortened word has had a letter dropped, as in a written abbreviation

parts.note: the name of the actor John Le Mesurier, of which a middle stretch is kept
taken as written; the middle letter then goes, as in the abbreviation n't

explanation.surface: An actor's role is one whose name must never be abbreviated.
explanation.walkthrough: John Le Mesurier was a British actor, best known as Sergeant Wilson in the TV comedy Dad's Army.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is a literary word for greedy or ravenous, from the Latin for being hungry.

clue.text: Sandglasses, say, for a little boy in French department

parts.note: e.g., for example, 'say'

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: the Gers is a department of south-west France
Tim is a short boy's name; Tiny Tim is Dickens's little boy

explanation.surface: Hourglasses, for instance, bought for a small boy in a French shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French department' looks like a shop section; it is a French administrative region.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg-timers are small sandglasses that run for the few minutes it takes to boil an egg.

clue.text: * Polly for the stocking she hasn't got

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the surname of Polly ..., a character in the poem
second meaning: a band holding up a stocking, which this free-living lady's name says she wears though she has none

explanation.walkthrough: Polly Garter is the warm-hearted young woman of Under Milk Wood who has many babies by different men.
explanation.definitionFit: A garter is an elastic band worn round the leg to keep a stocking up, and also Polly's surname.

clue.text: * Turn in pipe that was blind at night

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: a hose is a flexible pipe
U as in a U-turn

explanation.surface: A bend in a pipe that could not see a thing after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: In Under Milk Wood the sleeping town's houses are 'blind as moles' at night.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem pictures the dark town's dwellings with unlit windows, so each building was blind at night.

clue.text: Be familiar spirit for aristocrat

parts.note: a hob is a goblin or sprite, as in hobgoblin
nob is slang for a toff or aristocrat

explanation.surface: A witch's familiar spirit standing in for a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar spirit' reads as a witch's companion; 'Be familiar' is the definition and 'spirit' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix socially on friendly, easy terms, especially with people of higher status.

clue.text: Spoken initially, or spoken by a relative

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: belonging to or coming from a sister

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of the word
taken as written
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: Something said at the start, or said by a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is narrow: the relative in question is a sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Sororal means sisterly, of or from a sister, so it describes what is done by that particular female relation.

clue.text: * The sea was so 14 down (part 2), behind time, they say

definitions.note: the fruit names the shade of the poem's sloeblack sea

indicators.note: what they say is heard spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: behind time means running slow

explanation.surface: The sea was this black and running late, so people report.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 down part 2 is BLACK; the poem's sea is 'sloeblack, slow, black', and a sloe is a blackthorn berry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloes are the dark blue-black berries of the blackthorn, so the sea was sloe-black in the poem's description.

clue.text: See 11
See 11
Some opening for an artist with words and music

indicators.note: only some of the word is wanted, so its tail is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then cut down to its first three letters, the old poetic word ope
RA, Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A gallery opening for a painter, with speeches and music.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a dramatic work in which a libretto is set to a score and sung throughout.

clue.text: Jester to the Queen's kept on account of having the 14 down (part 2) stuff

indicators.note: what is kept is held within, so it goes inside the other word

parts.note: a clown is a jester
o/a, the abbreviation for on account
ER, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: The royal jester is retained on credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 down part 2 is BLACK, and the black stuff is coal.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal-owner possesses a mine and its coal, the black stuff, as in the old Welsh pit-owning class.
